q: In Annex A's General Definitions, what does “State” refer to?
n: “State – National Government.”

q: The Standards of Professional Practice (SPP) originates from which legal provision?
n: “Standards of Professional Practice (SPP) – from Article V Section 41 of RA 9266.”

q: “Commission,” as used in the SPP, refers to:
n: “Commission – PRC.” The Board, separately, refers to the PRBoA.

q: How often must an Architect's Certificate of Registration and Professional Identification Card (CoR/PIC) be renewed?
n: “Architect – Registered and Licensed Architect (RLA), natural person with CoR and PIC (renewable every 3 years).”

q: Which of these is NOT a role the term “Architect” can refer to under Annex A?
n: The Architect definition explicitly lists AOR, AICC, and CA as roles it can refer to. Project Manager is a role created under SPP 206, not part of this base definition.

q: An Architectural Firm (AF) organized as a sole proprietorship registers with:
n: “sole proprietorship for individual practice – registered to DTI,” while a professional partnership or architectural corporation registers with SEC and PRC.

q: Which statement about Architect vs. Architectural Firm is correct?
o: Both can be natural or juridical persons
Architect is always a natural person; AF is only a juridical person
AF is always a natural person; Architect is only juridical
n: The Architect is defined as a “natural person,” while the Architectural Firm is “only juridical person under Philippine law and jurisprudence.”

q: “RLPs” as defined in Annex A refers to:
n: “Professionals – Register[ed] and Licensed Professionals (RLPs), natural person with CoR and PIC.”

q: Under Annex A, which pair of terms is treated as meaning the same thing?
n: “Client, Owner and Project Proponent – meaning the same.” Separately, “Bid or Tender – meaning the same,” and “Contractor and General Contractor” also mean the same.

q: Under the General Notes on the Selection of the Architect, what determines the most appropriate method of selecting an architect?
o: The type and complexity of the project
The region where the project is located
n: “Most appropriate method of selecting an architect will depend on the type and complexity of the project,” and the scope of services also depends on the selection method used.

q: Which selection method is described as being “for relatively small project[s], based on reputation, personal or recommendations”?
n: Direct Selection is the method described this way, as opposed to Comparative Selection, which is conducted by committees through a multi-step process.

q: Put the steps of Comparative Selection in their correct order.
o: Invitation → Pre-qualification → Interview → Verification → Evaluation and Ranking → Negotiation
n: The six steps run: Invitation (with Terms of Reference), Pre-qualification (resume/portfolio), Interview (design methodology, not design itself), Verification (site visits), Evaluation and Ranking, then Negotiation of scope and fees.

q: During the Interview step of Comparative Selection, what does the architect explain?
o: His design methodology, not the design itself
The contractor he intends to hire
n: “Interview – architect explains his design methodology (not design).”

q: An Architectural Design Competition (ADC) is typically used for what kind of project?
n: “Architectural Design Competition (ADC) – used for civic or monumental projects (idea competition, design competition or design-build competition).”

q: Under Annex A, an ADC Jury must have at least how many members, and who assists in running the competition procedure?
o: 10 members; assisted by the Building Official
n: “Jury (at least 5 members, architect & sponsor/client).” The ADC procedure is “assisted by IAPOA; follows Archt's Guidelines.”

q: Which is listed as a disadvantage of the Architectural Design Competition method, per Annex A?
o: It is too fast to properly evaluate designs
It is expensive and time-consuming, and may discourage participants
It cannot be used for government projects
n: Disadvantages listed are: “expensive and time-consuming; may discourage participants; fraud clients/competitions.” The advantage listed is that it's “open to RLAs and AFs.”

q: Under SPP Document 201, what distinguishes Feasibility Studies from Pre-feasibility Studies?
o: Feasibility Studies use only secondary data; Pre-feasibility uses primary data
Feasibility Studies involve primary data and forecast project performance over time; Pre-feasibility relies on secondary data
There is no real difference between them
Pre-feasibility Studies are conducted only after construction begins
n: Pre-feasibility Studies use secondary data for early decision-making, while Feasibility Studies “involve[] primary data” and forecast “the performance of the project over time by gathering and analyzing primary data.”

q: Which Pre-Design service is described as an “analytical problem-seeking process to produce a statement and solution,” including a space program with space characteristics and costs?
n: “Architectural Programming – analytical problem-seeking process to produce a statement and solution; space program with characteristics of the spaces, cost etc.”

q: Value Management Studies, under SPP 201, aims to achieve what outcome?
o: The lowest possible design quality at any cost
An unimpaired program, system, or design at minimum cost with the same performance
A design that ignores budget constraints entirely
n: “Value Management Studies – applied in the cost management studies... achieving an unimpaired program, system or design at minimum cost with same performance.”

q: In Promotional Services under SPP 201, the architect acts in what capacity?
o: As an agent conducting and coordinating activities to promote the project, as the owner's professional representative
As a specialist consultant only, with no representative role
n: “Promotional Services – ...architect acts as an agent by conducting and coordinating activities for the promotion of the project (professional representative of the owner).”

q: Before rendering Pre-Design Services, what four things must the architect's proposal state?
o: Scope of work, manner of payment, owner's responsibilities, and other conditions
Only the fee amount and payment date
Scope of work and the architect's resume only
The names of all sub-consultants and their fees
n: The proposal must state: (1) scope of work, (2) manner of payment, (3) owner's responsibilities, and (4) other conditions.

q: Which method of compensation is notably NOT listed as an option for Pre-Design Services under SPP 201 (though it is available for Regular Design Services under SPP 202)?
o: Per Diem, Honorarium Plus Reimbursable Expenses
n: SPP 201 lists Multiple of DPE, Professional Fee + Expenses, Lump Sum/Fixed Fee, Per Diem/Honorarium + Reimbursable, and Mixed Methods — but not Percentage of PCC, since there's typically no construction cost yet at the pre-design stage.

q: In the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses formula, what does the Multiplier (M) compensate the architect for, and what is its typical range?
o: Overhead and reasonable profit; ranges 1.5 to 2.5
n: “M = Multiplier for head and reasonable profit (1.5 to 2.5 depending on architect's setup, expertise and complexity of the project).” Fee = Direct Cost × M.

q: Under SPP 201's reimbursable expenses (R), housing, transportation, and living allowance for consultants or technical staff apply when they are assigned to places how far from the area of operation?
n: “R = reimbursable expenses such as housing, transportation and living allowance of consultants or technical staff (if assigned to places over 100km from the area of operation), cost of printing of extra set of drawings...”

q: In the Per Diem, Honorarium + Reimbursable Expenses method under SPP 201, what specifically is an “Honorarium”, as distinguished from Per Diem and Reimbursement?
o: A fixed daily wage set by contract
A voluntary payment for which no charge was set
A percentage-based fee tied to project cost
n: “Per Diem – per day payment; Honorarium – voluntary payment (no charge was set); Reimbursement – out-of-pocket expenses such as travel, accommodations and subsistence.” Total Payment = Per Diem/Honorarium + Reimbursement.

q: Under SPP 202's applicability, which entities are NOT covered unless they are registered architectural firms?
o: BPOs and KPOs providing services for overseas clients
n: “not applicable to BPO and KPO providing services for overseas clients unless they are registered architectural firms.”

q: What three requirements must a foreign architect meet to practice regular design services under SPP 202?
o: A local counterpart RLA, malpractice insurance, and a government endorsement
Temporary/Special Permit (TSP) from PRC and DOLE, a Work Permit from DOLE, and a local counterpart who is an RLA
A Philippine passport, a PRC license, and 10 years' experience
None — foreign architects are automatically exempt from these requirements
n: Requirements: (i) Temporary/Special Permit (TSP) from PRC and DOLE, (ii) Work Permit from DOLE, (iii) a local counterpart who is RLA.

q: When do Regular Design Services, per SPP 202, officially begin and end?
o: Begin at groundbreaking; end at building turnover
Begin at project inception (analysis of owner's needs); end only at turn-over of the completed project to the owner
Begin at contract signing; end at issuance of building permit
Begin at schematic design; end at bidding
n: “regular services start at the project inception, from analysis and study of the owner's needs, preparation for the instruments of the service and supervision during project implementation, and ends only in the turn-over of the completed project to the owner.”

q: What document, based on current cost parameters, does the architect submit at the end of the Schematic Design Phase?
o: Statement of the Probable Project Construction Cost (SPPCC)
n: The architect “submits Statement of the Probable Project Construction Cost (SPPCC) based on current cost parameters” during Schematic Design, and this SPPCC is updated again at Design Development and Contract Document phases.

q: How many sets of construction drawings and technical specifications must be submitted for the purpose of securing a building permit?
n: “submits 7 sets of construction drawings and technical specifications for the purpose of building permit.”

q: Regarding bid documents furnished to bidders during competitive bidding, which statement is correct?
o: Bidders may reproduce bid documents freely once loaned
Bid documents are intellectual property; they are loaned (a bond may be required) and reproduction is not allowed
Bid documents become the bidder's property once submitted
There is no restriction on reproducing bid documents
n: “bid documents are intellectual property, returned (a bond may be required), reproduction is not allowed... documents used by the purpose agreed with the owner.”

q: Is the architect required to provide continuous 8-hour on-site supervision, and is he liable for the contractor's failure to carry out the contract documents?
o: No to both — 8-hour on-site supervision is not required, and the architect is not liable for the contractor's failures
8-hour supervision is required, but liability is waived
Liability applies, but 8-hour supervision is not required
n: “architect is not required to supervise on 8-hour on-site and shall not be responsible for the failures of contractor to carry-out the contract documents.” He does, however, report defects and condemn non-conforming work.

q: A “Certificate of Payment” issued by the architect certifies what, specifically?
o: That the work has progressed, is sufficient, and is in accordance with the contract documents, to the architect's best knowledge
That the building is ready for occupancy
That all reimbursable expenses have been paid
n: “Certificates of Payment – certification to the Client that the work progressed, sufficient and in accordance to the contract documents (to the architect's best knowledge).”

q: What is the key difference between a Single Contract and a Separate Contract manner of providing services under SPP 202?
o: Single Contract has no sub-consultants at all
Single Contract is between architect and owner with sub-consultancy contracts to other allied professionals; Separate Contract has separate owner contracts with each professional
Separate Contract merges all professional liabilities into one
n: In both cases, professional and civil liabilities of each State-regulated professional remain separate, but the contracting structure differs as described.

q: Group 1 under SPP 202's Project Classification covers buildings of the simplest utilization and character. Which of these belongs to Group 1?
n: Group 1 lists armories, bakeries, freight facilities, hangars, industrial plants, parking structures, public markets, service garages, and warehouses, among similar simplest-character buildings.

q: Which of the following is classified under Group 2 (moderate complexity of plan or design)?
n: Group 2 includes art galleries, banks, call centers, churches, city/town halls, college buildings and schools, dormitories, malls, and mixed-use buildings — moderate complexity.

q: Group 3 covers buildings of exceptional character and complexity. Which of these is a Group 3 building?
n: Group 3 includes aquariums, marinas, nuclear facilities, laboratories, auditoriums, airports, hospitals, hotels, and mortuaries.

q: Group 4 under the SPP's Project Classification refers specifically to:
o: Residences (single-detached, duplex, rowhouses, small apartments, townhouses)
Extensive detail projects like built-in components
n: “Group 4 – Residences (single-detached; single-attached or duplex; rowhouses or shophouses, small apartment houses and townhouses).”

q: Group 5 covers monumental buildings and similar facilities. Which of these belongs there?
n: “Group 5 – monumental buildings and other facilities such as: Exposition & Fair Buildings; Mausoleums, Memorials and Monuments; Specialized decorative buildings; Museums.”

q: Group 6 is defined by which characteristic?
o: Repetitive projects, where contract drawings are reused for repetitive construction without amending the drawing or specifications
Alterations and renovations to existing buildings
Housing subdivisions on a single site
n: “Group 6 – repetitive projects (contract drawings are reused for repetitive construction without amending the drawing and specifications).”

q: Group 7 specifically applies to which situation?
o: Housing projects: construction of several residential units on a single site using one set of plans, specs and related documents
n: “Group 7 – housing projects (construction of several residential units on single site) with use of one (1) set of plans or design, specifications and related documents.”

q: Group 8, “extensive detail projects,” covers which type of work?
o: Built-in components/elements, built-in equipment, special fittings, screens, counters, architectural interiors and development planning/design
n: “Group 8 – extensive detail projects such as: built-in components or elements, built-in equipment, special fittings, screens, counters, architectural interiors (AI) and development planning and/or design.”

q: Group 9 in the SPP's Project Classification applies to:
o: Alterations, renovations, rehabilitations, retrofit and expansion/additions to existing buildings belonging to Groups 1 to 5
n: “Group 9 – alterations, renovations, rehabilitations, retrofit and expansion/additions to existing buildings belonging to Group 1 to 5.”

q: Group 10 covers which kind of engagement?
o: Rendering opinion or giving advice, clarifications or explanation on technical matters pertaining to architectural works
n: “Group 10 – engaged in rendering opinion or give advice, clarifications or explanation on technical matters pertaining to architectural works.”

q: Under SPP 202, through whom should the Owner issue orders to the General Contractor?
o: Through a third-party project manager, always
n: “The owner should issue orders to the General Contractor only through the architect,” as part of the owner's duty for prompt examination and decisions to avoid unreasonable delay.

q: If the owner fails to implement the project after the architect has completed architectural plans/designs, specifications, and contract documents for the General Contractor, what percentage of his work is that considered, and what fee is he entitled to?
o: 50% of his work; entitled to 50% of the fee
75% of his work; entitled to 75% of the fee
90% of his work; entitled to 90% of the Architect's fee
100% of his work; entitled to 100% of the fee
n: “the Detailed Design and Contract Documents Phase of his services... is equivalent to 90% of his work. If the owner fails to implement the project, the architect is entitled to receive 90% of the Architect's fee.”

q: If construction is suspended for more than 6 months, what happens to the fee for the remaining construction-phase works?
n: “When construction is suspended for more than 6 months, the fee for the remaining works shall be doubled.”

q: Design of movable/fixed cabinets and other AI elements, site development plans, and urban design elements are compensated how, per SPP 202?
o: Included automatically in the base design fee
Not compensable under any SPP document
n: “Separate Services – the following services shall be compensated separately based on SPP Document 203: design of movable or fixed pieces of cabinets and other AI elements, site development plan (SDP), urban design elements, other items of similar nature.”

q: Who owns all drawings and contract documents signed and sealed by the Architect, whether the project is implemented or not?
o: The Architect — they remain his intellectual property under Sec 33 of RA 9266 unless a written agreement says otherwise
n: “Ownership of Documents – all drawings and contract documents signed and sealed are intellectual property and documents of the Architect (implemented or not), not to be reproduced or used in other work unless under written agreement with the Architect (Section 33 of RA 9266).”

q: Project Construction Cost (PCC), as defined under SPP 202, excludes which of the following?
o: Cost of materials and labor for architectural interiors
Fees for the Architect, the Engineer, and Specialist Consultants
n: PCC covers all construction-related costs (structure, fixtures, elevators, fire protection, AI, SDP elements) but “excluding professional and consultancy fees.” Project Development Cost (PDC), by contrast, is PCC plus all professional fees and other fees.

q: For purposes of SPP Document 203, the term “Architect” specifically refers to which role?
n: “For SPP Document 203, ‘Architect’ refers to ‘Consulting Architect.’” A CA is defined as “only RLAs who may have another professional license or may have a valid specialist certificate.”

q: What does the Architect's fee for extensive detailing of Architectural Interiors (AI) components get based on?
o: A percentage of the AI work's total cost
The same rate as Regular Design Services, with no adjustment
Man-hours billed at the DPE multiplier only
n: “For extensive detailing of AI components... Architect's fee shall be percentage of AI work total cost,” while any Engineering or Specialist Consultant fees remain separate from the architect's own.

q: Under Acoustic Design Services, the Consulting Architect works in cooperation with whom, who is described as the “prime professional hired by the owner”?
n: Acoustic Design Services are provided “in cooperation with the Architect which is the prime professional hired by the owner.”

q: For large-scale Site Development Planning (SDP), who must the Architect hire as additional support, per SPP 203?
o: Other RLPs as qualified Specialist Consultants (SCs)
n: “Ordinarily, the landscaping layout of small building projects could be done by an Architects as part of the SDP design. For large scale, the Architect must hire other RLPs as qualified Specialist Consultants (SCs).”

q: What is “Physical Planning,” as defined under SPP 203?
o: Only the structural engineering of a building
The orderly arrangement of vertical structures and horizontal developments (ROWs, open spaces, activity spaces), considering surroundings and neighboring impact
A synonym for Comprehensive Development Planning
n: “Physical Planning – orderly arrangement of vertical structures, horizontal developments like ROWs, open spaces and activity spaces, considering the immediate surroundings, interrelationship of structures and the impact on the neighboring areas.”

q: CDP services call for detailed study of which components, requiring the expertise of Specialist Consultants?
o: Physical, Economic, Socio-Cultural, Transport, and Legal/Administrative
n: The five components are Physical (land use/physical environment, mainly the MDP), Economic (nation's assets/management), Socio-Cultural (living conditions), Transport (movement of people/goods), and Legal and Administrative (relation to existing laws).

q: What are the two compensation options for Comprehensive Development Planning (CDP) Services?
o: Man-months, or as prescribed by the Architect's Guidelines
Hourly billing only, with no other option
n: “Manner of Compensation – two options: through man-months (for example, 22-man-days x 8-man hours and multiplied by a factor); as prescribed by the Architect's Guidelines.”

q: Which is NOT one of the three required characteristics of a building environment rating system under SPP 203?
n: The rating system must be credit-based (earning points for eco-friendly actions), flexible (projects need not meet identical requirements), and consensus-based/market-driven — not a rigid government mandate.

q: Forensic Architecture, under SPP 203, is described as what kind of study?
o: A legal review of contracts only
A scientific study on the built environment's well-being, focused on maintaining and prolonging the building's life cost-efficiently
A marketing analysis for building resale value
n: “The Architect in this area of practice undertakes a scientific study on the built environment's well-being, which allows the Architect to focus on the ways in which the building/structure can best maintain itself and prolong its life in a cost-efficient manner.”

q: What specific report, required under RA 9514 (the Fire Code of the Philippines), is included under the Post-Design specialized practice in SPP 203?
o: Fire Safety and Life Assessment Report (FALAR)
n: “Included under this Specialized Practice is the preparation of the Fire Safety and Life Assessment Report (FALAR) required by R.A. No. 9514, the 2008 Fire Code of the Philippines.”

q: Under SPP 203, an Architect specializing in Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) should preferably hold what status?
o: Membership in the IAPOA ADC Committee only
n: “An Architect specializing in ADR must preferably be State-accredited,” and the ADR modes covered are those prescribed under RA 9285.

q: Compensation for the various Specialized Architectural Services listed under SPP 203, all classified as additional/extra services, is generally computed how?
o: Only through a flat percentage of PCC
Through man-months (22 man-days × 8 man-hours, multiplied by a factor for overhead/indirect costs), or other applicable modes stated in Doc. 201, 202, or the Guidelines
Through a fixed government schedule with no adjustment
n: “Compensation for the foregoing specialized architectural services... shall be through man-months... or through any other applicable mode of determination of the Architect's fee as stated in Doc. 201, Doc. 202 and the Architect's Guidelines.”

q: Under SPP 204-A, who are the four principal members in the design and construction process?
o: Owner, Architect and SCs, Contractor, and the Supervision Group
Owner, Building Official, Contractor, and Bank
Owner, Contractor, Insurer, and the PRC
n: “For 50 years, four principal members in the design and construction process – the owner, the Architect and SCs, the Contractor and the Supervision Group.”

q: Who is normally responsible for recommending the Construction Supervision Group (CSG), and who hires them?
o: Recommended by the Contractor; hired by the Architect
Recommended by the Architect; hired by the Owner
Recommended and hired by the Owner alone
Recommended by the PRC; hired by the Owner
n: “The Construction Supervision Group (CSG) is normally recommended by the Architect and hired by the Owner. They report both to the owner and the architect.”

q: What are the four items in the Scope of Services for Fulltime Supervision under SPP 204-A?
o: Quality Control, Evaluation of Construction Work, Preparation of Daily Inspection Reports, Filing of Documents
Feasibility, Programming, Space Planning, Value Management
n: Scope of Services – Quality Control, Evaluation of Construction Work, Preparation of Daily Inspection Reports, Filing of Documents (with detailed tasks specified under the Architect's Guidelines).

q: Which of the following is a limitation placed on the Construction Supervision Group (CSG) under SPP 204-A?
o: The CSG may assume the Contractor's project superintendent role if needed
The CSG shall not assume the responsibility of the Contractor's project superintendent, nor decide on matters solely the AoR's responsibility
The CSG has unlimited decision-making authority over design changes
The CSG reports only to the Contractor
n: “The CSG... shall not assume the responsibility of the Contractor's project superintendent. The CSG shall not make decisions on matters that are the sole responsibility of the Architect-of-Record (AoR).”

q: Under Article 1723 of the Civil Code, and per SPP 204-A, the CSG's legal responsibility runs to whom, for what type of matters?
o: To the Owner for all matters, technical and administrative alike
To the Owner for administrative matters; to the Architect-of-Record for technical matters
To the Contractor for all matters
n: “The Construction Supervision Group (CSG) is responsible to the Owner only for administrative matters. For technical matters, the CSG is responsible to the Architect-of-Record (AoR).”

q: What degree, at minimum, must Inspectors of the Construction Supervision Group (CSG) hold?
o: A Bachelor of Science in Architecture (B.S. Arch.) degree
A master's degree in construction management
n: “Inspectors of the Construction Supervision Group (CSG) must have: A Bachelor of Science in Architecture (B.S. Arch.) degree,” plus extensive experience in design and building construction.

q: Who may serve as the Construction Manager (CM) under SPP 204-B?
o: A member of the Owner's staff, an independent individual, or a firm hired by the Owner — and the Architect himself may serve in this role
n: “Construction Manager (CM) could be: a member of the staff of the owner, independent individual or a firm hired by the Owner... The Architect can serve as the Construction Manager (CM).”

q: Which of these is NOT one of the four functions of the Construction Manager listed under SPP 204-B?
o: Design of the building's structural system
n: The CM's four functions are Coordination and Supervision, Cost and Time Control, Quality Control of Work, and Keeping of Records — mirroring CSG functions, not structural design, which remains the Architect/Engineer's role.

q: As Construction Manager, what is the Architect explicitly prohibited from doing?
o: Involving himself directly with the work of the Contractor (assuming the Contractor's liability), or imposing methods/systems/designs that substantially affect the construction schedule or impair his own design concept
n: The Architect as CM “shall not: involve himself directly with the work of the Contractor... [or] impose methods, systems or designs that will substantially affect the construction schedule and impair the design concept of the Architect.”

q: Under what condition does the Construction Manager (Architect) assume no liability for deficiencies in the manner of construction?
o: Never — the CM is always liable for construction deficiencies
Provided the CM faithfully discharged his functions during construction/project implementation
Only if the Owner signs a liability waiver
Only if construction is completed ahead of schedule
n: The CM assumes no liability for construction-manner deficiencies “provided the CM faithfully discharged his function/s during the construction or project implementation,” and similarly for design deficiencies provided the CM did not participate in that review/approval.

q: Who is generally considered capable of becoming a Construction Manager, per SPP 204-B's qualifications section?
o: Architects who are Contractors or have been in-charge of construction works
Only lawyers with a construction specialization
n: “Architects who are Contractors or have been in-charge of construction are usually capable of becoming Construction Managers (CMs).” The individual or firm principal must be a State-regulated professional, preferably an RLA in good IAPOA standing.

q: How are Construction Management Services compensated, relative to design services?
o: Bundled automatically into the design fee
Separately compensated from regular design services
Never compensated — considered a public service
Only through a fixed government rate
n: “Services of Architect as Construction Manager (CM) shall be separately compensated.”

q: Which incentive-type contract, appropriate during the initial stages of a project, adjusts the contract price upward or downward using a prearranged formula?
n: “Price Adjustment Provisions – the contract price is adjusted upward or downward using a prearranged formula. The operating and support cost factor provision provides a direct incentive on operating and support costs.” (Award Fee Provisions instead reward meeting cost-related target values.)

q: Building administration and management, per SPP 205, requires what kind of professional?
o: A multi-disciplinary professional who can perform a wide range of functions for efficient and economical operation and maintenance
Only a licensed real estate broker
n: “It requires the services of a multi-disciplinary professional who can perform a wide range or functions for the efficient and economical operation and maintenance of a building, facility or a complex.”

q: Under Building and Facilities Administration, what does the Building Maintenance Architect specifically formulate and enforce, especially during emergencies?
n: The Building Maintenance Architect shall “formulate and enforce rules on proper building usage (especially during emergency),” along with monitoring security and maintenance/upkeep services.

q: The study, research, and provision of solutions to discovered defects such as shrinkage and water seepage in a completed building is referred to as:
n: “study, research and give solutions to any discovered/emerging/evolving defects and failures such as shrinkage, water seepage and other problems in the building. This is referred to as ‘forensic investigation’ of the building's systems (Reference Document 203).”

q: What are the two listed methods of compensation for Post-Construction Services under SPP 205?
o: Percentage of gross rentals, maintenance and security fees; or Monthly salary/fee
n: “Percentage of gross rentals, maintenance and security fees” and “Monthly salary/fee” are the two methods explicitly listed for Post-Construction Services.

q: Comprehensive Architectural Services, per SPP 206, covers which five categories?
o: Only Pre-design and Regular Design Services
Pre-design, Regular Design, Specialized Architectural, Construction, and Post-Construction Services
n: “Comprehensive Architectural Services covers Pre-design Services, Regular Design Services, Specialized Architectural Services, Construction Services and Post-Construction Services.”

q: When an Owner hires an Architect or firm to coordinate the whole range of Comprehensive Architectural Services, what does this constitute?
n: “When the Owner hires and Architect or a firm to coordinate the whole range of Comprehensive Architectural Services (CAS), this constitutes Project Management (PM).”

q: In the Owner-Architect-Engineer-Contractor Team Approach, what is the Project Manager's (PM's) primary responsibility?
o: The exercise of overall cost control — planning, programming, and monitoring activities, advising on material costs and construction methods
n: “The Project Manager (PM)'s primary responsibility is the exercise of overall cost control. He will plan, program and monitor the various activities, and will act as an adviser on material costs and construction methods.”

q: In the Team Approach, who bears prime responsibility for the plan/design of the project?
o: The Architect and the Specialist Consultants (SCs)
n: “The Architect and the Specialist Consultants (SCs) will have prime responsibility for the plan/design of the project,” while Engineers handle their respective engineering plans and the Contractor is responsible for men, equipment, and delivery.

q: How is the Project Manager generally compensated, and what happens if the Architect-PM also performs regular design services on the same project?
o: Only through a fixed government rate; no separate compensation for design
On a percentage basis per the Architect's Guidelines; regular design services are compensated separately per SPP Doc. 202
Only through man-months; design services are bundled in
Never separately; PM services are always free
n: “The Project Manager is compensated on a percentage basis, described in the Architect's Guidelines. If the Architect as Project Manager (PM) performs regular design services for the same project, he shall be compensated separately for these services as stipulated in SPP Document 202.”

q: In Design-Build Services, what liability does the Architect assume that he does NOT assume under Regular Design Services?
o: Professional responsibility and civil liability for both the design AND the construction of the project
Liability only for the construction, not the design
Liability transferred entirely to the Contractor
n: “The Architect renders professional services in the implementation of his design. In Design-Build Services, he assumes the professional responsibility and civil liability for both the design and the construction of the project.”

q: Design-Build Services come in which two types or categories?
o: Design-Build Services by Administration, and Design-Build Services with Guaranteed Maximum Project Construction Cost
n: The two categories are Design-Build Services by Administration (covers the full Regular Design phases plus expanded construction-phase duties) and Design-Build Services with Guaranteed Maximum Project Construction Cost.

q: Under Design-Build with Guaranteed Maximum PCC, realized savings from the estimated PCC are divided how?
o: Equally between the Owner/Client and the Architect
n: “The Owner/Client is given an estimate of the project, and upon completion, if there are realized savings from the estimated project construction cost, it is divided equally between the Owner/Client and the Architect.”

q: If the actual cost exceeds the guaranteed PCC + 10% due to the Architect's own fault, up to what amount is the Architect liable for the excess?
o: Up to the amount of his administration fee
n: “Should the actual cost exceed the estimated PC + 10%, the Architect is liable for the excess amount but only up to the amount of his administration fee.” Costs from CVOs, EWOs, or NEDA-certified price escalation are instead borne by the Owner/Client.

q: Which pledge from the Architect's Credo must the Architect adhere to when involved in construction under Design-Build arrangements?
o: A pledge of exclusive loyalty to the Contractor
A pledge to disclose whenever required any business investment or venture that may create a conflict of interest, without compromising the Client's legitimate interest or impartial judgment
A pledge to waive all design fees
A pledge to always use the lowest-cost materials
n: The Architect “shall disclose whenever required, any businesses investment or venture that may tend to create a conflict of interest, and ensure that such conflict neither compromises the legitimate interest of the Client nor interfere with his duty to render impartial judgment.”

q: Under Design-Build Services, who pays directly for all labor and materials, and does the Architect advance money for these expenditures?
o: The Architect pays and later gets reimbursed
The Client pays all costs directly; the Architect does not advance money, though a revolving fund subject to periodic auditing may be given beforehand
The Contractor pays and bills the Architect
The Building Official manages all payments
n: “All costs for labor and materials are paid directly by the Client. The Architect does not advance any money for payment of expenditures connected with the work. Generally, a revolving fund is given to the Architect beforehand and is accounted for and subject to periodic auditing by the Client.”

q: Who is the “Professional Advisor” in an ADC, and what is their role?
o: A juror who casts the deciding vote
An architect nominated by the Owner and approved by IAPOA to organize the ADC on the Owner's behalf
A government auditor overseeing prize distribution
n: “Professional Advisor – an architect nominated by the Owner and approved by IAPOA to organize the ADC on behalf of the Owner.”

q: An ADC's classification as either “Project ADC” or “Ideas Competition” depends on what?
o: Whether it's open or limited by invitation only
Whether the ADC is for an actual project proposed for implementation, or a design/planning exercise to elucidate a problem
Whether the jury includes a lay member
Whether the competition runs one or two stages
n: “Project ADCs for actual projects proposed for implementation” versus “Ideas Competition or competition of ideas set as a design and planning exercise to elucidate a problem.” Project ADCs may separately be single-stage/two-stage and open/limited.

q: Before the Owner officially announces an ADC, what must be obtained through the ADC Committee of IAPOA?
o: Nothing — the Owner may announce freely
A written approval of the draft conditions, including timetable, registration fee, and jury membership
A signed contract with the eventual winner
n: “Before official announcement by the Owner, a written approval of the draft conditions (including timetable, registration fee and membership of the jury) shall be received by the owner through the ADC Committee of IAPOA.”

q: What are the size and composition rules for an ADC Jury?
o: Even number, no more than 10, no architect requirement
Odd number, not exceeding 7, with a majority who are architects, and at least one representing IAPOA
Exactly 5 members, all must be architects
No size limit, as long as the Owner approves
n: “The Jury shall be composed of the smallest reasonable number of persons and in any event should be an odd number and should not exceed seven (7); majority of the members should be architects. At least one of the Architect-Jurors shall represent the IAPOA. Maximum of (1) representative of the Owner.”

q: For a two-stage ADC, must the same Jury judge both stages?
o: No, a fresh jury is required for each stage
Yes — the same Jury should judge both stages of the competition
Only the chairperson needs to remain the same
It is optional, at the Owner's discretion
n: “In a two (2)-stage competition, the same Jury should judge both stages of the competition. In no case may a competition that has received IAPOA approval as a single-stage competition proceed to a second stage unless approved by IAPOA.”

q: May a member of the Jury take part in the ADC as a competitor?
o: Yes, as long as they recuse themselves from judging their own entry
No — no Jury member may compete, directly or indirectly, nor be commissioned with work connected to the prize-winning design
Yes, if approved by the Owner
n: “No member of the Jury will be allowed to take part in the competition, either directly or indirectly, nor be commissioned with work connected with the prize-winning design either directly or indirectly.”

q: Within what timeframe of the official ADC announcement must the Owner pay out the allotted prizes?
n: “The Owner undertakes to accept the decisions of the Jury and to pay the prizes allotted within one (1) month of the official announcement of the ADC results.”

q: If the winning Competitor of a Project ADC has no signed contract within 12 months of the results announcement, what happens?
o: The design becomes public domain automatically
The winner receives a further sum equal to the first prize; the Owner still cannot implement the project except with the winner's collaboration
The Owner is released from all obligations
The second-place winner is awarded the project instead
n: “provisions shall be made in the ADC Conditions for the first prize winner to receive compensation of a further sum equal to the amount of the first prize, if no contract has been signed within twelve (12) months... In so compensating the first prize winner, the Owner does not acquire the right to carry out the project except with the collaboration of its Author.”

s: SPP 208 · Copyright and Right of Ownership
q: Who retains the copyright of a plan/design submitted to an ADC?
n: “The author of any plan/design shall retain the copyright of his work; no alterations may be made without his written consent,” citing Secs. 20(4) and 33 of RA 9266.

q: For how long, as a general rule, must all ADC entries (including disqualified ones) be exhibited to the public, free of charge?
n: “All designs, including those disqualified by the Jury, shall be exhibited, as a general rule, for at least two (2) weeks, together with a copy of the signed report of the Jury. The exhibition shall be open to the public free of charge.”

q: In the event of a dispute unrelated to the adjudication process or prize awarding, how is it settled under SPP 208?
o: Direct litigation in court, skipping arbitration
Through an arbitration process approved by IAPOA, without initial recourse to litigation
The Jury decides unilaterally with no appeal
n: “In the event of a dispute, not related to the adjudication process or awarding of the prizes, the matter shall be settled by arbitration process approved by the IAPOA, and without initial recourse to any form of litigation.” The Jury remains the sole arbiter on adjudication/prize matters.

q: What presidential issuance, dated March 20, 1980, directed government agencies to prioritize members of Accredited Professional Organizations (APOs) in hiring professionals?
n: “March 20, 1980 – Marcos issued LOI No. 1000 which directs all government agencies to prioritize members of APOs in the hiring of professionals.”

q: According to SPP 209's Rationale, what is a key argument against relying heavily on foreign consultants?
o: Foreign consultants are legally barred from practicing at all
It entails expenditure of foreign exchange and is irrational since local technology/expertise is already adequate, displacing Filipino RLPs
Filipino architects lack the technical competence to compete
It is prohibited outright by the 1987 Constitution
n: “The full utilization of Filipino Professional Consultants can minimize the importation of foreign expertise (which entails expenditure of foreign exchange). Such importation is irrational... The competence of FPC (especially PCAs) is adequate and well-established.”

q: SPP 209's Declaration of Policy is grounded in which constitutional provision?
o: Section 14, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution
n: The Declaration of Policy quotes “Section 14, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution,” on sustained development of a reservoir of national talents and limiting profession practice to Filipino citizens save as prescribed by law.

q: What happens to an FPCA's status if he/she signs and seals architectural documents on a project?
o: Nothing changes; the FPCA has no added responsibility
He/she becomes the Architect-of-Record (AoR) and assumes the attendant responsibilities and liabilities
The project automatically becomes a Design-Build arrangement
n: “note: if the FPCA signs and seals architectural documents, he becomes the Architect-of-Record (AoR) and assumes the attendant responsibilities and liabilities.”

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six qualifications required for a Foreign Consultant (FC) or Foreign Architect (FA) under SPP 209?
o: Has a Temporary/Special Permit (TSP) per Secs. 37 and 38 of RA 9266
Is a registered/licensed professional in his own country of origin
Must hold a PRC license identical to a Filipino architect's
n: The six qualifications are: satisfies PCA definition; has a work/business permit per PRC guidelines; has acquired a TSP under Secs. 37–38 of RA 9266; is allowed by DOLE/BID to practice here; and is a registered/licensed professional in his own country — not a requirement to hold an identical PRC license.

q: The “Multiplier” under SPP 209 compensates the PCA for which combination of items?
o: Overhead costs, fringe benefits/social charges, fee for contingencies, interest on capital reserves, and profit
n: The Multiplier covers all five: overhead costs of the office, fringe benefits and social charges, fee for contingencies, interest on capital reserves, and profit — and it “varies according to the types of architectural consulting work.”

q: Which of the following IS listed within the Scope of Professional Architectural Consulting Services (PACS)?
n: PACS scope includes program/project conceptualization, technical advice/consultation, teaching/lecturing/coaching/mentoring, R&D, documentation, feasibility studies, land use planning, construction management, post-construction evaluation, and CPE training — not government regulatory functions.

q: If a Professional Consulting Architect (PCA) is a juridical person, what must the firm hold, in addition to SEC/DTI registration?
o: A PRC-issued certificate to operate as a registered architectural firm
A separate PACS license from the DTI
n: “if juridical person, SEC-registered partnership/corporation or DTI-registered sole proprietorship... Note: the consulting firm must have PRC-issued certificate to operate as a registered architectural firm.”

q: If no Filipino Professional Consulting Architect (FPCA) is available for a specialization, and a non-FPCA is engaged, what condition must be met?
o: No condition — non-FPCAs may be freely engaged
At least 2 Filipino RLAs shall be employed as understudies
The non-FPCA must waive all professional fees
Only government projects may engage non-FPCAs
n: “Only duly-qualified FPCAs for fields of specialization under the CBNE. If no FPCA is available, non-FPCA... is allowed as long as at least 2 Filipino RLAs shall be employed as understudies.”

q: Under the Salary Cost × Multiplier method for PACS compensation, what multiplier factor is specified?
n: “Salary Cost X multiplier + (direct cost/reimbursable expenses) – Multiplier – factor of 3.0.” This method suits cases where costs are hard to pre-determine, but cannot be used when services aren't measured by length of time worked (e.g. creative works).

q: When are PCA fees for late payment entitled to interest, and per what standard?
o: Immediately upon any delay, at a fixed 10% rate
Late payments of more than 30 days from billing, at the rate set by BSP/IAPOA or as mutually agreed
Interest is never charged on late PACS payments
n: “Interest Due on Late Payment of Fees – late payments of more than 30 days from billing shall be entitled to interest (as set by BSP, IAPOA or when agreed by the PCA and client).”

s: SPP 209 · Seal and Use of Seal
q: Under what condition may a PCA sign and seal architectural documents in a PACS engagement?
o: Only if the PCA is a foreign consultant
Only if the PCA also acts as the Architect-of-Record of the project
Any PCA may always sign and seal documents
Never — sealing is reserved to the CSG
n: “the PCA can only sign and seal architectural documents if and only if he also acts as the Architect-of-Record of the project.”

q: What is the general rationale of the Architect's Guidelines (UAP-IAPOA Document 210), per Rule I?
o: To eliminate all prior SPP documents
Standardizing the architect's compensation and complementing other regulatory laws
To set criminal penalties for unlicensed practice exclusively
To regulate only government construction contracts
n: “Section 2: Rationale – standardizing the architect compensation and complement other regulatory laws.”

q: Which of these is listed among the “other considerations on professional fees” under Rule II's Criteria section?
o: Time schedule and potential changes; other professional input; client's procedure/timing; administration costs; probability of contingencies; number of parties consulted
n: These six factors are explicitly listed as additional considerations layered on top of the base criteria of talent/skill/experience and type/scope/complexity of services.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule II, Method of Compensation
q: How many main types of Method of Compensation does Rule II, Section 4 recognize?
o: Three: percentage-based, lump sum/fixed, and time basis
n: “it has three main types – percentage-based, lump sum/fixed, time basis,” though methods can be combined or modified for specific cases.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule II, Percentage-Based Fee
q: What are the three options for determining the Project Construction Cost (PCC) used in a percentage-based Professional Fee?
o: Estimated, Awarded, and Final PCC (PPCC, APCC, FPCC)
Only the Final PCC is ever used
n: Probable PCC (PPCC, mutually agreed based on unit price parameters), Awarded PCC (APCC, based on the winning contractor's bid), and Final PCC (FPCC, based on submitted cost records).

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule II, DAEDS vs DADS
q: What is the minimum percentage that a DADS (Detailed Architectural Design Services) contract's architectural fee must represent, relative to the equivalent DAEDS fee?
n: “the architectural design services for this contract [DADS] shall be at least 60% of the fees in DAEDS contract,” since DADS excludes engineering fees while the architect remains the lead coordinator.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule II, Lump Sum
q: For Lump Sum or Fixed Fee compensation, what should the Service Agreement state regarding time and changes?
o: Nothing — lump sum contracts never need a time limit
A time limit for the service, and a provision for additional compensation for extra time on changes ordered after approval
Only the final total price, with no other terms
n: “It is recommended that the Service Agreement states the time limit of the service and provision for additional compensation for extra time for changes ordered by the Client after the approval.”

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule II, Time Basis
q: Time Basis compensation is typically used for which kinds of services?
o: Services that are difficult to determine in advance, or interim/short in duration — e.g. pre-design services, expert witness work, or specialist consultancy
n: “Time Basis – charged on a mutually-agreed hourly (man-hours) or daily (per diem) or per month rate. Applicable if the services are difficult to determine in advance, or if interim or short in duration.”

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Pre-Design Fees
q: Prior to starting Pre-Design Services, what acceptance fee does the Architect request upon signing the agreement, and within how many days must the Client pay subsequent billings?
o: 5% acceptance fee based on the agreed PF; payment within 7 days
No acceptance fee; payment within 30 days
n: “the Architect requests for a 5% acceptance fee based on the agreed PF upon signing of the agreement... the Client shall pay the payments upon the request of the client within 7 days from submission of the statement of account.”

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, RPF Groups
q: For a Group 1 building (e.g. a warehouse) under a DAEDS contract, with a PCC of ₱50M or less, what is the Recommended Professional Fee?
n: Group 1's RPF for DAEDS at 50M and less is 5% (3% for DADS, being 60% of the DAEDS rate).

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, RPF Groups
q: For a Group 2 building (e.g. a school) under a DAEDS contract, with a PCC of ₱50M or less, what is the Recommended Professional Fee?
n: Group 2's RPF for DAEDS at 50M and less is 6% (3.6% for DADS).

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, RPF Groups
q: For a Group 3 building (e.g. a hospital or hotel) under a DAEDS contract, with a PCC of ₱50M or less, what is the Recommended Professional Fee?
n: Group 3's RPF for DAEDS at 50M and less is 7% (4.2% for DADS) — the highest sliding-scale starting rate among Groups 1–3, reflecting exceptional character and complexity.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, RPF Groups
q: What flat DAEDS Recommended Professional Fee applies to Group 4 (residences, small apartment houses, townhouses), regardless of PCC?
n: “Group 4 Projects: small residentials, apartment houses and townhouses – regardless of cost – RPF for DAEDS: 10% of PCC; RPF for DADS: 6% of PCC.” Unlike Groups 1–3, this rate does not slide with PCC brackets.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, RPF Groups
q: What flat DAEDS Recommended Professional Fee applies to Group 5 (museums, mausoleums, monumental buildings), regardless of PCC?
n: “Group 5 Projects... regardless of cost – RPF for DAEDS: 12% of PCC; RPF for DADS: 7.5% of PCC.”

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, RPF Groups
q: Under Group 6 (repetitive projects reusing the same contract documents), what percentage of the original RPF applies to the Second Building in the series?
n: Group 6's schedule: First Building = 100% of RPF; Second Building = 50%; Third Building = 40%; Fourth and succeeding buildings = 30% — subject to major adjustment if site conditions differ significantly.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, RPF Groups
q: Group 8 (extensive detail projects: built-ins, special fittings, screens, counters, architectural interiors) carries what flat Recommended Professional Fee?
o: It varies entirely by negotiation, with no baseline
n: “Group 8... Recommended Professional Fee (RPF) – 15% of the PCC.”

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, RPF Groups
q: Group 9 (alterations, renovations, rehabilitations, retrofit, and expansion of existing buildings under Groups 1–5) carries what Recommended Professional Fee?
n: “Group 9... Recommended Professional Fee (RPF) – 150% of the RPF,” reflecting the added complexity of working within/around an existing structure.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, RPF Groups
q: For Group 10 (rendering technical opinions/advice, e.g. consultations), what is the minimum RPF for a consultation, and for serving as an expert witness?
o: ₱1,000/hour consultation; ₱5,000/appearance (whether the hearing happens or not)
n: “Minimum RPF for consultations – Php 1,000 per hour... Minimum RPF for being expert witness – Php 5,000 per appearance (whether the hearing happened or not).” These figures reference October 2014 peso values.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Unit Cost Method
q: In the Unit Cost Method example (10,000 sqm GFA office building, ₱30,000/sqm, 6% RPF), what unit rate is applied to the Non-GFA portion relative to the GFA rate?
n: “For the PF unit cost of Non-GFA (use 50% of PF of GFA): P900/sqm,” against the GFA unit cost of P1,800/sqm (6% × P30,000/sqm).

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Manner of Payment
q: Under the cumulative Manner of Payment schedule, what percentage of the Professional Fee should have been paid by the completion of the Design Development Phase?
n: Cumulative schedule: 5% at signing → +15% (20% total) at Schematic Design → +20% (40% total) at Design Development → +50% (90% total) at Contract Documents → remaining 10% split between construction-phase liability (5%) and periodic supervision (5%).

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Manner of Payment
q: Within the Bidding and Negotiation Phase, within how many days after awarding to the bidder should the PF be adjusted to 90% based on the winning bid?
n: “within 15 days after the awarding to the bidder, the PF shall be adjusted so that it will amount to 90% of the PF computed from the lowest or winning bid.”

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Manner of Payment
q: The remaining 10% of the Professional Fee, chargeable during the Construction Phase, is broken down how?
o: 10% for supervision only, nothing for liability
5% for Architect's Liability and 5% for Periodic Construction Supervision
All 10% is withheld until final Certificate of Occupancy
n: “Construction Phase – the remaining 10% of the PF is broken down as follows: 5% for Architect's Liability; 5% for Periodic Construction Supervision.”

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Fee Adjustment Factors
q: Which of the following is explicitly listed among the Fee Adjustment Factors that can increase or decrease the architect's Professional Fee?
o: The architect's personal preferences on color schemes
Project Delivery Method and Construction Procurement (e.g. Design-Bid-Build vs Design-Build vs PPP)
The season of the year construction begins
n: Listed adjustment factors include Scope of Services, Project Delivery Method/Procurement, Construction Schedules, Documentation/BIM, Specialist Consultants, Approvals, New Technologies, Construction Administration, Site Conditions, Renovation vs New Construction, Repeat Work, and more.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Specialized Services Fees
q: For Architectural Interior, Acoustic Design, Architectural Lighting, and Site Development Planning services, what is the Recommended Professional Fee range under Rule III?
o: 2% to 5% of the cost of work
10% to 15% of the cost of work
20% to 25% of the cost of work
A flat 8% regardless of cost of work
n: “For Architectural Interior (AI), Acoustic Design, Architectural Lighting Layout and Design, and Site Development Planning (SDP) – Recommended Professional Fee (RPF) – 10% to 15% of the cost of work.” Payment runs 30% at preliminary design, 50% at final design, and 50% at project completion.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Physical Planning Fee
q: Under the Physical Planning fee schedule (for building sites like industrial estates or subdivisions), what is the basic rate per square meter for the first 5 hectares?
n: “Basic rate for the first 5 hectares – P5.00 per sqm – P250,000” flat, dropping to P4.00/sqm (5–10 has), P3.00/sqm (10–50 has), and P1.50/sqm beyond 50 has. Rugged/steep terrain adds 20–30%.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Physical Planning Payment
q: In the Physical Planning payment schedule, how is the RPF split across the Framework Development Plan, Conceptual Master Development Plan, Preliminary Master Development Plan, and Detailed Master Development Plan?
n: FRDP: 30% of RPF; CMDP: 30% of RPF; PMDP: 20% of RPF; DMDP: 20% of RPF.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Fulltime Supervision Fee
q: What is the Recommended Professional Fee for Full-Time Supervision Services (SPP 204-A) under Rule III?
n: “Recommended Professional Fee – 1% to 1.5% of PC.” The Architect may also bill Specialist Consultant coordination at 5% of the SC's fee, if hired separately by the Client.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Construction Management Fee
q: What is the Recommended Professional Fee for Construction Management Services (SPP 204-B) under Rule III?
n: “Recommended Professional Fee – 1.5% to 3% of the PCC,” notably higher than the Fulltime Supervision range because it carries broader coordination, cost, and time-control responsibilities.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Post-Construction Fee
q: If Post-Construction Services compensation is based on value-pricing, what is the Recommended Professional Fee range?
n: “if based on value-pricing, 4% - 6% of gross rental. This incentive-type of management fee will ensure more efficient and economical operation and maximize building revenues.”

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Comprehensive Services Fee
q: What is the Recommended Professional Fee range for Comprehensive Architectural Services (SPP 206) as Project Manager?
n: “RPF = 2% to 5% of PCC.” If the PM also performs regular design services, that portion is compensated separately.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule III, Design-Build Fee
q: What is the Recommended Professional Fee for Design-Build Services by Administration, versus Design-Build with a Guaranteed Maximum Cost?
n: “For DBS by Administration – 7% of the PCC (exclusive of Regular Design Services RPF); For DBS on a Guaranteed Max. Cost – 10% of PCC or built-in in the GMC (exclusive of Regular Design RPF).”

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule IV, General Conditions
q: Under Rule IV, who is prohibited from lawfully collecting fees for architectural services?
o: Any architect regardless of license status
No one — fee collection is unregulated
n: “Unlicensed or unregistered person collecting fee for architectural services is unlawful under RA 9266.”

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule IV, Late Payment Interest
q: Under Rule IV, on what basis is interest computed for architect's fees unpaid beyond 30 days from billing?
o: A flat 12% annual rate set by RA 9266
The prevailing rate set by the BSP, mutually agreed upon by the Architect and Client
10% of the total unpaid amount, flat
No interest is charged — only late fees apply
n: “the Architect is entitled for interest at the prevailing rate set by the BSP and mutually agreed upon by the Architect and his client, on all fees... not paid within 30 days from receipt of billing.”

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule IV, Government Taxes
q: The Professional Fee stipulated under the Methods of Compensation and Schedule of Fees is described as “net.” What does this mean regarding taxes?
o: Income tax is included in the PF, but VAT is carried by the Architect
Any tax such as VAT (except income tax) shall be carried by the Owner
All taxes, including income tax, are the Owner's responsibility
No taxes apply to architectural services at all
n: “the PF stipulated... is net which means any tax i.e. VAT (except income tax) shall be carried by the Owner.” Income tax remains the Architect's own personal obligation.

s: Architect's Guidelines · Rule IV, Professional and Civil Liability
q: What may the Architect secure, where applicable, commensurate with the magnitude of their project involvement and compensation?
o: A performance bond from the Contractor
A professional liability/malpractice insurance policy or its equivalent in bond form
n: “where applicable, the Architect may secure locally their professional liability insurance or malpractice insurance or their acceptable equivalent in bond commensurate with the nature magnitude of their project involvement and compensation.” This cost is chargeable as part of total project cost.

q: What is the correct sequence of dispute-resolution steps under Rule IV, Section 19, before litigation is even considered?
o: 14-calendar-day negotiation → 14-calendar-day mediation/conciliation → CIAC arbitration (6-month guaranteed resolution)
Court filing first, then optional CIAC review
Mediation only, with no arbitration option
n: Parties “may venture into a 14-calendar-day negotiation period,” then if that fails, “14-calendar-day mediation/conciliatory discussions,” then may “seek for arbitration modes of ADR under the Construction Industry Arbitration Commission (CIAC) that guarantees resolution within 6-month period.”

q: Where are CIAC arbitration proceedings under Rule IV held?
o: The CIAC Office at corners Sen. Gil Puyat Ave. and Makati Ave., Makati City
n: “ADR proceedings shall be at the CIAC Office at corners Sen. Gil Puyat Ave. and Makati Ave. in Makati City.” A losing party may file a Petition for Review before the Court of Appeals.

q: Who prepares amendments to the Architect's Guidelines, and where must the final amendment be submitted for approval?
o: Any individual architect; approved directly by the PRC
A Special Committee on the SPP of the IAPOA, in consultation with PRC-PRBoA; submitted to the UAP National Board for Approval
The Building Official; approved by the DTI
The Contractor's association; approved by DOLE
n: “amendment to this document shall be prepared by a Special Committee on the Standards of Professional Practice of the IAPOA, in consultation with PRC-PRBoA and other association of architects. Amendment shall be submitted to the UAP National Board for Approval.”

q: “Cost of Work (CoW),” as defined in Annex A, refers to what?
o: The total cost of fixtures and accessories for architectural interiors, acoustics, lighting works, and site development civil works designed/specified/procured by the Specialist Architect and SCs
The contractor's total labor bill only
n: “Cost of Work (CoW) – total cost of fixtures and accessories for architectural interiors, acoustics, lighting works, site development civil works (hardscape and softscape) designed, specified or procured by the Specialist Architect and the SCs.” This is used for some Specialized Architectural Services fee computations.

q: Who is the “Prime Professional,” as defined in Annex A?
o: Any engineer working on the project
The Architect commissioned to plan/design the building and coordinate the works of all allied design professionals, ensuring compatibility with the architectural design concept
n: “Prime Professional – refer to the Architect commissioned by the Owner/Client to plan and design the building/structure and all its utilities and to coordinate the works of all allied design professionals involved.”

q: What must a “Service Agreement,” as defined in Annex A, formally be?
o: A duly notarized written contract or equivalent public instrument stipulating scope of services and guaranteeing compensation
An email exchange confirming the scope of work
A handshake agreement witnessed by two parties
n: “Service Agreement – means a duly notarized written contract or equivalent public instrument stipulating the scope of services and guaranteeing compensation of such services to be rendered by an architect registered and licensed by the PRC-PRBoA.”

q: Which items are explicitly included under “Overhead,” as defined in Annex A?
o: Provisions for office/light/air-conditioning, depreciation/rental of equipment, vehicle/travel expenses, office supplies, taxes/insurance (other than salary-related), library/periodical expenses, and non-project-specific admin salaries
n: Overhead is a broad category covering office operating costs, equipment depreciation, non-salary taxes/insurance, professional development expenses, and general executive/administrative salaries not tied to a specific project.

q: Which Republic Act is the source law establishing the Alternative Dispute Resolution Act referenced throughout the SPP and Architect's Guidelines?
n: RA 9285 is the Alternative Dispute Resolution Act of 2004. RA 8293 is the Intellectual Property Code, RA 9184 is the Government Procurement Reform Act of 2003, and RA 9266 is the Architecture Act of 2004.

q: Which Republic Act is the Architecture Act, under which the SPP itself (per Article V, Section 41) and the licensure of architects are established?
n: RA 9266 is the Architecture Act of 2004, establishing the PRBoA, licensure requirements (CoR/PIC), and Section 41 mandating the SPP itself.
